evidences.title: Does Tony Abbott always make the same speech? | Tony Abbott | The Guardian
evidences.content:
The Australian prime minister's speech at Davosstruck a familiar tone and was criticised for being inappropriately partisan. So does he stick to the same themes whoever the audience? We compare four speeches in wordle form

To see the wordles more closely, go to our gallery

In prime minister Tony Abbotts most recent speechto the assembled heads of state at the World Economic Forum at Davos, heurged the worlds government to get out of the way of businesses while having a dig at Australias previous Labor government for their spending habits.
  It felt like we might have heard it before.
  Guardian Australia has compared four of Abbotts major speeches since the election campaign kicked off in August last year to see what words he most oftenuses and if there is really thatbig a difference in each of his speeches.
  A wordle shows in graphic form which words in a speech are used most frequently. The bigger the word appears in the "word cloud", the more often it has been repeated. 
  Perhaps unsurprisingly, but also somewhat ironically for a prime minister in favour of small government,the word government was one of the most frequently repeated words in the speeches we compared.
  Tax, Labor, Australiaand peoplewere also hot contenders for his most-used word, as the four wordles below reveal.

In the analysis of Abbotts World Economic Forum address, he threw around the words infrastructure, global, trade, Australia and G20 the most.
  Smaller mentions went to strengthen, sustainable, India and China. They were the only other countries to score a mention in the wordle, though Brisbane also got a look in. One could speculate on what Queenslands capital has in common with India and China, but the more boring (and honest) answer is that it is hosting Novembers G20 summit.

Moving on to Abbotts address atthe Coalition'selection 2013 campaign launch, Labor was the third most mentioned word, demonstrating Abbott's highly negative style of campaigning.

When Abbott travelled to Tasmania, he quite astutely mentioned the state in his address to the states Liberal party councilmore than he talked about any other state or territory in Australia. People, government and tax continued to be favoured topics.

The final speech we put through wordle was the address to the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry annual dinner. No prizes for guessing that business was a top word in that particular outing. Not one for surprising people, Abbott's other most-used words were government, people, Australia and of course, tax.
